newsitem.title: CHILE: Chile suspects guerrilla escape got help from abroad.
newsitem.headline: Chile suspects guerrilla escape got help from abroad.

text.p: Four left-wing guerrillas who escaped from a maximum security jail in a helicopter may have been helped from abroad by another Latin American rebel group, Chilean authorities said on Thursday.
A judge investigating the spectacular escape on Monday said there could have been "a prompt operation from abroad to bring these people out."
Judge Lamberto Cisternas questioned employees of a rental firm that owned the helicopter used to hoist the men from the jail yard in the middle of a gun battle with prison guards.
The employees said the helicopter was hired by a man who spoke with a heavy Argentine accent and two women thought to be from the United States.
Police sources quoted by La Tercera newspaper said they believed armed leftist groups in Latin America were exchanging information and could be acting in tandem.
They said there could be a link between the storming of the Japanese ambassador's residence by Marxist guerrillas December 17 and the Chilean jailbreak two weeks later.

The escaped guerrillas belonged to the Manuel Rodriguez Patriotic Front (FPMR), which took up arms against General Augusto Pinochet's military regime in 1983. They were in jail for a failed assassination attempt on Pinochet in 1986 and the murder of right-wing senator Jaime Guzman in 1991.
The escape from the modern, heavily-fortified jail caused Chile's civilian government huge embarrassment. National prisons director Claudio Martinez resigned in disgrace.
Police set up roadblocks and tightened controls at border crossings, ports and airports but have yet to find traces of the escaped rebels or their accomplices.

Interior Minister Carlos Figueroa said the men were in Chile, but an FPMR spokesman who described himself as Comandante Fabian said in a television interview that they had been smuggled out of the country within hours of the escape.
Business leaders and right-wing politicians sharply criticised the government and the prison system for being caught off-guard by the well-planned operation.
"It's a joke that this efficient country ... builds a prison from which terrorists can escape like angels in the sky," said Pedro Lizana, president of the industrial trade group Sofofa.
